#4736 1 2005-10-13T00:25:30Z Maniac
TUMIKI Fighters for Mac
TUMIKI Fighters for Windows

This has been passively mentioned in game threads for other Kenta Cho games, but now that it's been released for Mac, I must say, TUMIKI's pretty fun.

For those of you who don't know, this game's another shoot-em-up. You drive this little plane, and you shoot up other planes with the Z key, which will then cause the planes to fall down. The small planes die immediately, and if you catch it it'll stick to your plane and fire against the enemy when you're firing. It also gives you points while you're firing. However, one shot from a bullet and it's destroyed, so use the X key to pull the pieces in temporarily.

Your main plane flies on the left side of the screen, and can be destroyed by one bullet, so it pays to gather up pieces for shielding, if nothing else

Larger ships tend to fire more projectiles at you, and are also composed of multiple pieces which break off as their health bars(lower right of screen) run out. Again, catch the pieces to get them working on your side, but they'll be destroyed by other bullets.

At the end of each stage, you'll confront a boss plane, which is usually composed of four or more pieces which take a long time to destroy, and fire *lots* of particles at you. Yes, you can catch the pieces as they fall off too

When you destroy the final boss piece, it'll fall down, but you can't catch it. It'll explode, and then your plane will take off all its acquired pieces, and speed off towards the next stage.

Here are two screenshots:





It's a really fun game, so I suggest everyone go download it.

Finally, for you veterans, I noticed everyone was stuck on Level 3. I don't know why. I know it's a pretty difficult thing, as I've seen, but you really need to start wisely positioning and rotating your pieces before you catch them. The boss is rather tricky, but possible.

My high score is getting to the last piece of the Level 4 boss

#116929 14 2005-11-22T02:28:27Z Maniac
Well, no, but rocket launchers in particular suck up a lot of memory because each frame they:

1. Look for the player
2. Find out if there's a rocket on the screen already
3. If it can see the player, and a rocket isn't on the screen already, fire a rocket
4. Move a rocket if it's on the screen(which isn't a simple algorithm, mind you)

And that's just a single rocket launcher. Put a whole lot in there, along with gauss turrets and drones, and your computer slows down enough for you to notice.

Oh yeah. I must say, this one's a tricky one.

Basically, in this level you're going to start having to get familiar with rockets, as well as multidodging. Multidodging is my affectionate name for the technique of actively avoiding multiple elements at once. In this case, the rocket and the various mines in the arena. You want to sort of pay attention to the rocket, and dodge it, while also making sure you land on bounceblocks so you don't hit mines.

If all of the above didn't make sense, trial and error works. Don't worry, the 20's gets fairly rough quickly.

EDIT:

As in, don't worry, it's not your fault, everyone has trouble on these levels.

#118521 37 2005-11-27T17:24:57Z Maniac
I only had 6, but they were rather difficult ones.

1. This map. "Just Over the Horizon" is the name of Stage 2 of Tumiki Fighters. I thought that one was fairly obvious, but I guess not

2. This map. "Coo-ee!" was what you had to recognize here. It's from a Sherlock Holmes case, the Boscombe Valley Mystery. "Coo-ee!" was the personal call that the lord (I forget his name) used to call his son.

3. This post. "By any stretch of the means" is a Rick-ism from the book Crash.

4. This post. "Holy convoluted metaphor!" This came from this Bunny comic originally. However, Daddaluma and others have pointed out that Robin actually says this in the original Batman shows, and that Bunny ripped the actual quote.

5. This map. "Ickle" is an adjective stolen from the game Airburst Extreme.

Uh, unfortunately I forgot what the sixth reference was. But these five ultimately show that my references were way too obscure for anyone to realistically get.

If I may contribute the coding portion of the laser drone, laser drones use the concept of raycasting to find the ninja. If the ray doesn't hit any tiles, and it hits the ninja, then the small beam is formed, and you've got a second to get away before it turns into the deadly one.

#127791 2 2005-12-29T01:22:16Z Maniac
What you want to do is search your computer for a .sol file. It's a file that Flash uses to store data, such as your progress in this case.

To find the .sol file:

1. Boot up your Windows search (I'm assuming you're using a Windows. If not, reply and I can give you Mac directions)

2. Check "Search for Hidden Files"

3. Search for *.sol

If no files come up, your progress has been irrevocably lost.

#129732 3 2006-01-04T20:31:41Z Maniac
Yes, I have. A (small) explanation from the DROD site:

Quote: What is DROD?
What is DROD? Greater minds than ours have faltered and failed at those three little words. We're not entirely sure, ourselves - DROD can't be described in terms of other games without just confusing the issue. It's a puzzle game without block pushing or falling bricks. It's a turn based RPG without the role-playing or statistics. It's an action game without the action. It's a roguelike that really has little in common with Rogue and its cousins. It's rare that someone makes a game that can't be described as something-meets-something else, and it's almost impossible to describe to someone without sitting them down and just showing them the game.

And we wouldn't have it any other way.

I might need a piece of paper, though.

You play a little ugly man, named Beethro, with an oversized sword. Like other characters with oversized swords, Beethro has an odd haircut and a job to do which will make him lots of cash -  to get to the bottom of the dungeon, killing everything in his path, without dying himself.

The dungeon is made up of a lot of rooms - kill all the monsters in a room, and it stays clear. Clear all the rooms on a level, and you're allowed access to the next one. Often, you can enter and leave the rooms as much as you like, although it will reset the room if you haven't finished it. Every room is divided up into a grid - you can have only one thing in a square of the grid at a time (Beethro, his sword, a monster, a pit, and so on). Beethro will die as soon as one of the many denizens of the dungeons attacks him, and he's only got his sword for protection.

Of course, Beethro has an advantage. Unlike aforesaid games with characters with oversized swords, Beethro is experienced in killing all sorts of creatures, so it only takes waving the sword in their square to kill them; and Beethro has as much time as he needs to decide what to do. Every turn, he decides whether to move (using the number pad by default), wait (using the 5 on the number pad), or rotate his sword 45 degrees (using Q for clockwise and W for anticlockwise by default), and the game will pause while you decide his next step. Beethro makes his move, then the monsters (many puzzles taking advantage of this fact), so what could have been a frantic, and nigh on impossible, game of hack-and-slash becomes a violent but intelligent puzzle game.

And DROD has some of the toughest puzzles you'll ever see. Some will have you collapsing trapdoors and opening doors; some will have you coaxing invincible monsters into dead-ends; some will have you turning the monsters own attacks against them. And the last handful has you going up against their leader, the 'Neather, who delights in slamming doors in your face and sending wave after wave of monsters to kill you. It's a touching tale that parallels most of our daily existence, and the path to take to break free of our mundane existence and live the life we've always wanted. It's a cunning parable that would make Confucius proud. Let me explain.

The roaches symbolise our mundane problems - credit card debt, bills, the dog next door that just won't shut up - and the roach mothers the root of these problems, which is yourself. The evil eyes represent those problems that you never plan for but should. There are plenty of people who will help you if you let them once you've sorted out the mundane, but are soon followed by those that are vindictive just when you don't need it. You may feel like you're in the rat race, but some smart maneuvering will ensure you keep out of the way of the larger problems that restrict so many. Let your affection grow, don't get trapped by the small things, and keep a careful eye out for things that don't spring up onto you until it's too late.

Ermacrules29

Ermacrules appeared, at first, to be one of the average denizens of the Internet. He made his debut posting in the Favorite Curse Phrase topic in the Bash and Thrash. This would be one of his few intelligent posts.

After that, his second post was quoting the massive amount of text in this test thread without contributing anything at all.

This was where his destructive path began. He devoted the next few posts of his existance solely to advertise his own site without first establishing himself in the community. Then, he started promoting Mortal Kombat (the game where he got his avatar and nick from Ermac, one of the characters).

After this, he started one of his legendary tacky webcomics, Ermacs adventure comics. Soon after that, he made his legendary What is N? topic.

It all went downhill from there. Members were generally agitated at Ermac's inability to accept criticism and change, and ideas, though he did manage to implement him, generally were not worked on for more than about two minutes.

Eventually, he did attempt to change a little bit, making a small animation request topic. But by that time the damage was done, and the entire forum was against Ermac. He was banned by majority vote in a ban poll, and established the first "'Blizz ban" by getting Kablizzy to personally make a sarcastic remark about him being banned.

Morals:

  • Read a bit before asking on the forums. We generally like to donate our time to things that haven't already been answered.
  • Don't diss N, especially seeing as this is the N forum
  • And for goodness sake, spend time on such touchy works as webcomics.
  • Finally, listen to criticism and change based on it, or you will generally get the forum on your bad side.

*bump*

I've been doing Hell speedruns with my new Snake instead of the Spur, and I can tell you this: while it seems a step backwards at first, it really helps. For starters, the level 1 Snake does more damage than a level 1 Spur shot, and that's without leveling it up. There's just enough XP in the capsules at B1 to level the Snake to 2 (which suggests that Pixel was encouraging this combination for speedruns )

However, this means that you can't charge up the Snake and do a bunch of damage, either, so you have to start using Curly more often to take out the starblocks and do the heavy damage. But it frees up Quote to set off the Deleets that they're not able to get to yet.

Ballos takes quite a bit longer to defeat, mainly because of, again, the lower damage of the Snake. However, it still proves handy in that you can quickly level it up with the green flying bats, and you can either shoot Ballos with it or shoot Ballos with Curly's Nemesis.

Even with the relatively sloppy run I had (since I haven't got as much experience using the Snake) I still managed a 4'54", which was only ten seconds slower than my top Spur run of 4'44".

#134817 4 2006-01-22T22:58:20Z Maniac
HeartView already discovered this glitch. I forget the URL of his map submission, though.

Basically, the reason this happens is that, when a seeker drone sees you, it automatically calculates what terrain it will hit at the end of its "rush" and then rushes forward until it hits it. If it hits the ninja on the way, great!

Anyway, when the ninja triggers the trapdoor, the seeker drone doesn't update its view of the world - in its mind, it still thinks the far wall is as far as it will go, so it will then go through the trapdoor. After rushing, it then "comes to its senses" and goes back and forth in its little prison.

Another corollary of this "feature" is that if a seeker drone heads towards you and would hit a door at the end, and the door is then open when it's done, it will stop temporarily and then go through.

#147662 5 2006-02-23T23:47:09Z Maniac
Alrighty then. Here's what to do:

1. Make two seperate areas with 1-wide dead-end passageways somewhere in them. Put launchpads in the end of these. Place the pad the ninja will exit out of first, then the one the ninja will hit.

2. Delete all walls in between the two areas.

3. Go to the text box with your level code in it. Go to the end of the code. You should see something like the following:
2^xcoordinate,ycoordinate,xacceleration,yacceleration

The 2^ means it's a launchpad, and the first two variables represent its location. The last two represent x and y acceleration.

4. Positive numbers launch the ninja up and to the right, negative numbers launch the ninja down and to the left. Type in different numbers into the xacceleration and yacceleration fields, then load the level.

5. Go down the narrow corridor, then enter frame-by-frame mode. Hit the launchpad, then note where the first and second frames of the ninja are.

6. Mess with the x and y acceleration until the ninja hits the other launchpad in the second frame.

7. Congrats! You now have a fully functional one-way teleporter.

Yeah... this wouldn't actually be as hard to implement as, say, diagonal doors, because of the way N is coded. If you'd like to learn more about doors, read Tutorial B Section 2.

Anyway, you'd just have to do something like this (pseudocode):

IF ninja.location = timerswitch.location THEN
 openappropriatedoor();
 doorstimed = doorstimed + 1
 doortimer[doorstimed] = 1
END IF
...
FOR I = 1 TO (doortimer array size)
 IF doortimer[I] = 1 THEN
 timer[I] = 1
NEXT I
...
FOR J = 1 TO (doortimer array size)
 IF timer[I] = 1 THEN
 START TIMER (timerlength as defined by user)
 WHEN TIMER IS DONE shutappropriatedoor();
NEXT J

Wow. That's a lot of pseudocode. But it wouldn't be *that* difficult, I should think.

#8402 1 2006-05-01T19:19:07Z Maniac
As you all know, I was in Florida for a week about a few weeks ago. During said time, I had access to a Windows computer.

Warning Forever

Download it here

Awesome, awesome, awesome to the power of twelve. This game boils down the entire genre of "your ship shoots other things" to the most potentially awesome part, the boss fights, dueling the huge ship with you the puny one. In each phase, you take on a boss ship with multiple destroyable parts, weapons and a core. After defeating it, you get points and bonuses, and then you move on to the next one.

Oh, but it's not that simple. Each boss gets harder than the last, obviously, but they evolve in response to whatever you focus on. Spending a lot of time getting rid of the lasers so you won't die so often? The next one has more. Going for the core quickly? The connecting points by it are gonna get much stronger. The bosses can also get a bunch of arms to swat at you with, several deadly weapons, and even boosters to just slam into you and destroy you. It's an awesome game. Get it now.

Jumper Two

Download it here!

This game is a real gem. You're this hideous block-shaped abomination with only one goal - to escape. According to forum legend Brickman, it's "similar to what N might look like if all of its levels were designed by Killisk." To get around from stage to stage, you've just got to do one thing. Jump.

Each stage poses several puzzles to impede you from your goal, and as you solve the stages, the environment changes and a story is laid out. The graphics, while not amazingly super-duper-Halotastic, get the job done and still look pretty good. The music is to die for. And what with sixty included levels, and a level editor for importing your own sagas, you'll never get tired of it.

=======

Well, to be honest, those two games were so good I didn't have time to check out a third. Play them.

  • For everybody to play: Windows, Mac and Linux are all supported!
  • Large amount of control over what you're doing without being super-complicated
  • People who will smack you around then tell you why.
Cons:

  • Occasional lag
  • Computer practice mode is way different than multiplayer
Gate 88 is just a great game to play. It's the reason Eli never comes here anymore. Get hooked today!

#218961 8 2006-08-24T00:02:46Z Maniac
Quote: Ngaged, August 23, 2006 07:09 pm
you can view a replay of what happened before your death.

Actually, no you can't. The demo system is completely deterministic - meaning that it only records key presses, and nothing else.

This means that the game doesn't actually know where the drones are and what the turret status is at any time - it just plays out the keypresses and computes normally. Meaning that things such as playing the demo backwards and starting in the middle don't work - there are an infinite number of ways the past could have gotten to the future.

Therefore, I feel completely justified in spending even less time than that playing it. If you want to make it interesting, so that more people are interested in playing your game, you've got to do better than ten minutes.

If everybody "wasn't bothered" to delete all the objects so you could reset, almost every game in existence would be reduced to this level. Name any one game you play regularly, and there's a function to start over without unloading the program and reloading it again. Why? Because the programmers spent time on it.

Now, I understand the value of working with easy objects first, but you don't do things because they're easy. You do things because they're awesome. Now come back after spending a month on this and I bet it'll be a much better game. And a very awesome game is better than a hundred small 10-minute games, eh?

#287111 2 2007-01-18T12:02:00Z Maniac
I can't really answer the first few questions, but I can help with the algorithm.

Basically, O(n) means that this algorithm is a recursive one, and it's on the order of n squared. This means that it calls itself more and more times each time it recurses, eventually approaching some multiple of n squared for whatever input you supply the algorithm.

This means that it's not an incredibly efficient algorithm, but it's a lot better than if it were in logarithmic or polynomial time.

Yes, that's java, but you'd need to add that into a class file and add the main(String args[]) method to the class in order to put it in a program.

Beyond that, it's fuzzy. I haven't studied how Java interacts with other languages very much.

If you wanted variable writing, you'd need to do something like this instead - not very difficult for a programmer of your calibre I assume?

import java.io.BufferedWriter;

public static void writeToFile(String outfile, String content)
{
   try {
      BufferedWriter out = new BufferedWriter(new FileWriter(outfile));
      out.write(content);
      out.close();
      }
   catch (IOException e) {
         //do something with the GUI to tell the user that something bad happened
         System.exit(0);
   }
}

You might want to take a look at the System object documentation to look at some of the stuff you can do with Java and the operating system.
